from pathlib import Path
from pypdf import PdfReader
out = Path('tmp/pdfs')
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
r = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
print('Metadata:',r.metadata)
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
    s = p.extract_text()
    (out / f'page-{i+1:02d}.txt').write_text(s)
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'=== PAGE {i+1} ===\\n'+p.extract_text() for i,p in enumerate(r.pages)))
print((out/'manuscript.txt').read_text())
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a practical failure of image stitching: changing the seam alone cannot repair underlying misalignment. Selectively aligning problematic patches and reconnecting their seams is a useful, modular refinement strategy.

Figures 1, 7, 10, and 11 demonstrate visible improvements to curbs, stairs, and other structures. Evaluation covers 79 image pairs across three datasets, includes computational comparisons, and reports 108 first-place votes out of 160 judgments for the proposed method.

The pipeline is understandable at a conceptual level, and established methods and public datasets are credited. Section 4.4 and Figure 12 provide a helpful, candid account of failures involving widespread misalignment and large displacement.
weaknesses: The central flow modification is insufficiently specified. Section 3.4 denotes it as f(V), but Equation (4) defines a scalar sigmoid of spatial position without explicitly defining the resulting vector field. Warp orientation, overlapping-patch handling, and SIFT-flow settings also need clarification. Fixing graph-cut boundary labels preserves source assignments but does not itself guarantee continuity of warped image content across patch boundaries.

The seam acceptance rule in Section 3.3 can accept uniformly poor alignment: if every evaluation error equals 0.4, max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) holds and refinement is skipped. An absolute quality criterion or evidence validating this heuristic is missing. Moreover, the small-local-parallax assumption in Section 3.4 and dependence on partially successful initial alignment support a narrower scope than the introduction's claim of almost removing the rough-alignment requirement.

The methodological advance over prior seam-quality evaluation [17] and seam-guided alignment [18] is incremental and insufficiently isolated experimentally. Figure 4 illustrates sigmoid settings qualitatively, but there are no controlled quantitative ablations establishing the benefits of selective patch extraction, flow tapering, and seam recomputation over simpler dense-flow refinement alternatives.

Quantitative comparisons cover only two seam-cutting methods from 2018–2019. Comparisons with seam-driven methods [18,26] are principally illustrative, while relevant cited alignment approaches such as [9,12] are not evaluated. This leaves the claimed advantage over competing parallax-handling approaches inadequately established. Integration with different alignment and seam-cutting backbones is also asserted rather than demonstrated.

The main metric in Equation (5) closely follows the SSIM criterion used to select repairs and does not measure geometric distortion or content preservation. The manuscript itself identifies a disagreement between this metric and perceived quality. The user study offers complementary evidence, but its eight manually selected 'controversial' cases, unspecified presentation randomization, and lack of uncertainty estimates limit the generality of its conclusions.

There are secondary reporting inconsistencies: legends in Figures 6, 8, and 9 identify methods [21] and [19], whereas the text describes [17] and [16]. Table 1 gives 159 rankings for [17] and 161 for [16], although the stated protocol implies 160 per method. These need correction, but they do not explain the substantial preference margin or independently determine the rejection recommendation.
